Incorrect - Inhibition of microtubule polymerization and neutrophil migration describes the mechanism of colchicine, not probenecid.
Incorrect - Xanthine oxidase inhibition describes the mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, not probenecid.

Correct - Probenecid is a uricosuric drug that blocks proximal tubule reabsorption of uric acid, thereby promoting its excretion in urine and lowering serum uric acid levels; it can also block penicillin secretion in the urine.
questions.overview: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that lowers serum uric acid by blocking proximal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its urinary excretion; it can precipitate uric acid kidney stones and, as a sulfa drug, was originally developed to reduce renal secretion of penicillin and thereby prolong its effect.

questions.stem: Factor H is a plasma glycoprotein that protects host cells from inappropriate complement activation via which mechanism?
options: Binding C1q to prevent classical pathway activation
Blocking mannose-binding lectin from binding microbial surfaces
Accelerating decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) and inactivating C3b
Cleaving C5 to prevent membrane attack complex formation
explanations: Incorrect - Factor H acts on the alternative pathway C3 convertase, not on C1q or the classical pathway.
Incorrect - Factor H does not interact with mannose-binding lectin, which is part of the lectin pathway.

Correct - Factor H is a liver-synthesized glycoprotein that protects host cells by accelerating the decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) and promoting cleavage/inactivation of C3b; some pathogens (H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, streptococci, Pseudomonas) hijack Factor H to evade the alternative pathway.
Incorrect - Factor H acts upstream at the level of C3 convertase, not by cleaving C5.
questions.overview: In the alternative complement pathway, spontaneously generated C3b is normally rapidly destroyed unless stabilized on a pathogen surface, where it forms the C3 convertase (C3bBb) that amplifies C3b deposition. Factor H is a host-protective regulatory protein that accelerates decay of this convertase and inactivates C3b on host cells; several pathogens exploit Factor H binding to evade complement-mediated killing.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops a swelling behind the knee that later ruptures, causing calf pain and swelling that mimics a deep vein thrombosis. This describes which of the following?
explanations: Incorrect - A tophus is a uric acid deposit seen in chronic gout, not a synovial cyst of the knee.
Incorrect - A ganglion cyst is a distinct, generally non-inflammatory cystic swelling near joints/tendons, not the classic RA-associated popliteal cyst described.
Correct - A Baker's (popliteal) cyst is a synovium-lined sac continuous with the joint space at the back of the knee, commonly seen in RA; rupture can produce symptoms mimicking a DVT.
Incorrect - Rheumatoid nodules are subcutaneous nodules typically on the elbow, associated with RF-positive RA, not fluid-filled popliteal masses.
questions.overview: A Baker's (popliteal) cyst is a synovium-lined sac at the back of the knee that communicates with the joint space, commonly occurring in rheumatoid arthritis due to increased synovial fluid production; rupture can mimic the presentation of a deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: Primary biliary cirrhosis, characterized by T-cell mediated destruction of small bile ducts, is most strongly associated with which rheumatologic condition?
explanations: Incorrect - Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel vasculitis associated with hepatitis B, not PBC.

Correct - Primary biliary cirrhosis is associated with limited scleroderma, with 5-15% of PBC patients having limited scleroderma (also associated with Sjögren's, lupus, RA, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis).
Incorrect - Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy with no described association with PBC.
Incorrect - The described association in the notes is specifically with limited (not diffuse) scleroderma.
questions.overview: Primary biliary cirrhosis is a T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts leading to cholestasis (elevated conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase), pruritus, and potential progression to cirrhosis. It shows a notable association with limited scleroderma, as well as Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, RA, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following metabolic conditions is most classically associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD)?
explanations: Incorrect - Von Gierke disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) is associated with gout via lactic acidosis-driven uric acid retention, not CPPD.

Correct - Hemochromatosis, a hereditary iron overload disorder, is classically associated with CPPD, with calcium pyrophosphate deposition seen in up to two-thirds of hemochromatosis patients along with iron deposition in synovial tissue; hyperparathyroidism and joint trauma are other associated conditions.
Incorrect - Wilson disease (copper overload) is not among the associated conditions for CPPD described in these notes.
Incorrect - Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency) causes excess uric acid production and gout, not CPPD.
questions.overview: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) causes asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis, acute pseudogout attacks (rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals), or chronic pseudo-osteoarthritis, typically in older patients. It is associated with joint trauma, hyperparathyroidism, and hemochromatosis, the last of which causes CPPD via associated iron deposition in synovial tissue.

questions.stem: The Schirmer test, used in the evaluation of suspected Sjögren's syndrome, directly measures which of the following?
options: Radionuclide uptake by the salivary glands
explanations: Incorrect - Salivary flow is assessed by whole sialometry (collecting and weighing saliva), a separate test from the Schirmer test.
Incorrect - Radionuclide uptake is assessed by salivary gland scintigraphy, not the Schirmer test.

Correct - The Schirmer test uses filter paper placed near the lower eyelid to measure the amount of tear wetting over 5 minutes, assessing reflex tear production, which is reduced in Sjögren's syndrome.
Incorrect - Antibody titers are measured by serologic testing, not the Schirmer test, which is a physical/functional ocular test.
questions.overview: Sjögren's syndrome causes lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands, producing dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia). Diagnostic criteria include objective measures of these deficits — the Schirmer test for tear production and salivary scintigraphy/sialometry for salivary flow — alongside anti-SSA/SSB antibodies or biopsy showing lymphocytic sialadenitis.

questions.stem: The heavy chain V, D, and J gene segments that rearrange to generate B-cell receptor diversity are located on which chromosome?
explanations: Incorrect - Chromosome 6 harbors the HLA/MHC genes, not the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus.

Correct - The immunoglobulin heavy chain V, D, and J gene segments are located on chromosome 14, and their combinatorial rearrangement, along with light chain rearrangement, generates the enormous diversity of B-cell receptors from a limited number of genes.
Incorrect - Chromosome 11 is not the site of heavy chain gene rearrangement described in these notes (it is associated with the ATM gene in ataxia telangiectasia).
Incorrect - Chromosome 22 is associated with the 22q11 deletion in DiGeorge syndrome, not the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus.
questions.overview: B-cell receptor diversity arises not from one gene per receptor but from combinatorial VDJ rearrangement of a limited set of variable (~50), diversity (~25), and joining (~6) gene segments on chromosome 14 for the heavy chain, combined with light chain V/J rearrangement, generating millions of unique antigen receptors.

questions.stem: Conjugate vaccines against encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Hib, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae) improve immunogenicity primarily by which mechanism?
options: Using a live attenuated form of the polysaccharide-encapsulated organism
Linking the polysaccharide antigen to a protein carrier, enabling T-cell help and stronger B-cell memory
Directly stimulating B cells without any antigen presentation
Bypassing the need for antibody production entirely
explanations: Incorrect - Conjugate vaccines are not live attenuated organisms; they combine a purified polysaccharide antigen with a protein carrier.

Correct - Polysaccharide antigens alone activate B cells in a T-cell-independent manner, producing a weak, short-lived, mostly IgM response with poor memory; conjugating the polysaccharide to a protein carrier allows the protein to be presented to T cells, which provide help to B cells, producing a stronger, class-switched, memory response.
Incorrect - The mechanism specifically involves T-cell-dependent activation via the conjugated protein, not purely direct B-cell stimulation.
Incorrect - The goal of vaccination, including conjugate vaccines, is to generate a strong, durable antibody (and memory) response, not to bypass antibody production.
questions.overview: Polysaccharide capsule antigens activate B cells independent of T-cell help, generating a weak, transient IgM-predominant response without memory. Conjugate vaccines attach the polysaccharide to a protein carrier so that T cells can be recruited to help B cells, producing a stronger, longer-lasting, class-switched antibody response with immunologic memory.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis with skin involvement confined to the fingers and face, calcinosis, and telangiectasias. She now presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion. Echocardiogram shows right ventricular enlargement and elevated pulmonary artery pressure. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her current presentation?
options: Pulmonary hypertension, the leading cause of death in limited scleroderma
Primary biliary cirrhosis causing hepatopulmonary syndrome
Scleroderma renal crisis with malignant hypertension
explanations: Incorrect - Myocarditis/conduction disease is described with diffuse scleroderma, not the limited/CREST form.

Correct - In limited scleroderma (CREST), pulmonary hypertension (and interstitial lung disease) is the main risk and leading cause of death, even though the disease course is otherwise more benign than diffuse disease.
Incorrect - PBC is associated with limited scleroderma but causes cholestatic liver disease, not primary pulmonary hypertension.
Incorrect - Scleroderma renal crisis is a complication of diffuse, not limited, scleroderma, and presents with acute renal failure and marked hypertension, not isolated pulmonary hypertension.
Incorrect - Esophageal dysmotility is part of CREST but causes reflux/dysphagia, not right heart strain and pulmonary hypertension.
questions.overview: Limited (CREST) scleroderma generally has a more benign course than diffuse disease and rarely involves the heart or kidneys, but pulmonary complications — particularly pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung disease — are the leading cause of death. Routine monitoring includes echocardiography to detect early pulmonary hypertension.
